## tus-node-server: how resumable state is tracked server-side

**Answer: the server core is stateless; resumability is delegated entirely to the `DataStore` you plug in. With `@tus/file-store` (the default disk store), offset is persisted and derived from the on-disk file length — not held in memory. Metadata is persisted to a JSON info file. Only the default locker is in-memory.**

Important structural fact first: since 1.0.0 the project is a monorepo — `tus-node-server` the package is deprecated ("considered unstable and will only receive security fixes"), and the current packages are `@tus/server`, `@tus/file-store`, `@tus/s3-store`, `@tus/gcs-store`, `@tus/azure-store`, `@tus/utils` ([README note, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)). There is no `lib/` anymore.

### The state model

- `Upload` is the unit of state: `{ id, size?, offset, metadata?, storage?, creation_date? }` — `offset` is the authoritative resume position ([Upload.ts#L1-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/Upload.ts#L1-L12)).
- The abstract `DataStore` contract (in `@tus/utils`, not `@tus/server`) defines `getUpload(id)` with the doc comment: *"Called in HEAD requests. This method should return the bytes writen to the DataStore, for the client to know where to resume the upload"* ([DataStore.ts#L40-L52](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/models/DataStore.ts#L40-L52)). The base implementation returns a zero-offset stub — i.e., the server never tracks progress itself.
- The HEAD handler does exactly two things state-related: `file = await this.store.getUpload(id)` under a lock, then `res.headers.set('Upload-Offset', file.offset.toString())` ([HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L16-L23), [HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/handlers/HeadHandler.ts#L45-L47)). It also reports `Upload-Length`/`Upload-Defer-Length` from the same object.

### `@tus/file-store` — persisted, disk-derived offset

- **Create**: writes an empty file at `directory/<id>` and persists the full `Upload` JSON via a configstore — `await fsProm.writeFile(filePath, ''); await this.configstore.set(file.id, file)` ([index.ts#L70-L80](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L70-L80)). Default configstore is `FileConfigstore` ([index.ts#L32-L46](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L32-L46)), which is just `FileKvStore` re-exported ([configstores/index.ts](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/configstores/index.ts)) — it writes `<id>.json` next to the upload: `await fs.writeFile(this.resolve(key), JSON.stringify(value))` ([FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L9-L12), [FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/utils/src/kvstores/FileKvStore.ts#L29-L31)).
- **Write (PATCH)**: opens the same file with `fs.createWriteStream(file_path, { flags: 'r+', start: offset })` — appends at the exact client-reported offset — counts bytes through a transform, and returns the new `offset + bytes_received` ([index.ts#L97-L128](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L97-L128)).
- **Read (HEAD/resume)**: `getUpload` does NOT trust any in-memory counter. It re-reads the JSON info file for `size`/`metadata`/`creation_date` and then **`offset: stats.size`** — the actual byte length from `fs.stat` ([index.ts#L130-L165](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/file-store/src/index.ts#L130-L165)). So the source of truth for the resume offset is the persisted file itself; a process restart loses nothing.
- This "file + adjacent info file" layout is documented as the universal store pattern: *"All stores (as in the `datastore` option) save two files, the uploaded file and an info file with metadata, usually adjacent to each other"* ([server README, pinned](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).

### Where memory is used (and isn't)

- The default **locker** is `MemoryLocker` — `locks = new Map<string, LockEntry>()` in-process ([MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/src/lockers/MemoryLocker.ts#L32-L34)); README says explicitly: *"By default it uses an in-memory locker... When running multiple instances of the server, you need to provide a locker implementation that is shared between all instances (such as a `RedisLocker`)"* ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- In-memory KV stores (`MemoryKvStore`, re-exported as `MemoryConfigstore`) exist but are intended as caches for cloud stores (e.g. `@tus/s3-store` `cache:` option) — the README's KV-store section only shows `MemoryKvStore` used as an S3 metadata cache, never as the source of truth ([server README](https://github.com/tus/tus-node-server/blob/cdd6e7937cb451c9f5591ece602645b143eb0a58/packages/server/README.md)).
- Conclusion for the report: **persisted** for FileStore (offset = file size on disk, metadata = JSON sidecar); **in-memory only** for the default lock and for optional cloud-store caches.

I read this as a read-only leak investigation - I traced cross-file state and browser/process teardown and identified the safest isolation boundary.

## Conclusion

The exact full-suite root cause is **inconclusive** because WP4’s failure assertion was unavailable. I found no persistent profile, service-worker, port, or Chrome leak that explains both failures.

The strongest explanation is **resource/handle accumulation in the long-lived, non-isolated Bun test process combined with fragile browser teardown deadlines**. The browser harnesses themselves already run in fresh Node subprocesses, so isolating their Bun wrapper files from the other 67 files is the lowest-risk deterministic fix.

## Concrete findings

- `package.json:23` runs all 69 files in one Bun process without `--isolate`.
- Bun 1.3.14 explicitly provides `--isolate` so leaked globals and handles from one test file cannot affect another.

Specific cleanup defects can accumulate before the browser gates:

- `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:133` and `:192` open SSE response bodies but never consume or cancel them. Service processes are killed in `afterEach`, but the parent-side fetch streams are not explicitly released.
- `services/projection-gateway/test/realtime-wss.test.ts:163` calls asynchronous `server.stop(true)` without awaiting it.
- Several successful waits create uncancellable `AbortSignal.timeout()` timers. Most are bounded to 2–10 seconds, so they are real transient retention rather than a convincing multi-minute root cause:
  - `tests/e2e/durable-main-restart.test.ts:35,83`
  - `tests/e2e/runtime-routes.test.ts:27`
  - `services/projection-gateway/test/events-http.test.ts:27`
  - `apps/stage/src/App.test.tsx:57,70`

WP3 teardown has a more serious failure-path flaw:

- `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.harness.ts:947-984` waits only five seconds for natural Chrome exit.
- If that deadline expires at `:975`, execution skips service termination and profile cleanup at `:984-987`.
- Thus the reported “Chrome process exit timeout” is primarily a brittle cleanup assertion; once triggered, it also creates an actual process/resource leak.
- CDP disconnect and OS process exit are separate events. Under complete-suite pressure, Chrome can disconnect correctly but take over five seconds for its process tree to terminate.

WP4’s harness is cleaner:

- It uses Playwright-owned `chromium.launch()` and `browser.close()` at `tests/e2e/windows-topology.harness.ts:888`.
- Its module-level `process.on("unhandledRejection")` at `:3` is never removed, but this module runs in a one-shot Node subprocess, so it cannot accumulate across the 69 Bun files.
- Profiles and service workers are not shared: WP3 uses a PID-qualified clean profile; WP4 uses ephemeral browser contexts.

Happy DOM is not the primary leak:

- Registrations in the React tests pair `GlobalRegistrator.register()` with an awaited Promise-returning `afterAll(() => GlobalRegistrator.unregister())`.
- `tests/setup.ts` is no longer a Bun preload; it is imported only by `UpdateCoordinator.test.ts`.
- Some tests leave window listeners attached, but unregistering Happy DOM closes that window after the file.

## Lowest-risk deterministic change

Split the heavyweight browser wrappers into fresh Bun invocations:

1. Run the ordinary suite while excluding:
   - `tests/e2e/prepared-evidence.test.ts`
   - `tests/e2e/windows-topology.test.ts`
2. Run WP3 in a fresh Bun process.
3. Run WP4 in another fresh Bun process.

This preserves every assertion, remains sequential, and introduces no sleeps, retries, skips, or weaker deadlines. It is stronger than merely adding `--isolate`, because each browser gate receives a fresh OS process and heap.

Secondarily, harden WP3 cleanup by using Playwright-owned `launchPersistentContext()` or by force-terminating and awaiting the Chrome process tree after CDP shutdown instead of failing before the remaining cleanup executes.

## Inspection performed

Reviewed package/Bun configuration, all browser wrappers and harnesses, process-spawning E2E tests, model-isolate lifecycle, Bun servers, SSE/WebSocket readers, Happy DOM registration, global mutations, AbortSignal timers, profile/artifact paths, and relevant cleanup history. I ran only static searches, process inspection, and `bun test --help`; no full or browser suite was run.
